text: Welcome. You’ve just said goodbye to Anne and Green Gables, and a new book is close. Before we open it, we spend this week on the true history behind it. Today’s question is how World War Two began, and who started it. First you’ll warm up and do some word work. Then a short reading, and a few questions to answer in your own words.

Today’s reading move is a bit like packing for a trip. A novel set in real history expects you to bring some facts along. As you read, collect the names of countries, leaders, and dates, like things going into a suitcase. When the story starts next week, you’ll be glad they’re already packed.

The top sentence is a model, and every capital in it is there for a reason. Look at the names of places, months, and people. The bottom one has lost all of its capitals, and it’s really two sentences squeezed into one. Find where one thought ends and the next one begins.

Four kinds of word work today. Some of it asks you to notice before anyone tells you the rule, and that’s on purpose. A rule you find yourself stays with you longer than one you’re handed. So go slowly at the start, look hard, and make your best guess before you check.

This week we’re building a bridge, one word at a time. Two small word parts at the front of words will do the building. One means across, and one means forward. Read each meaning first, then choose the part that fits. Every right choice lays a plank. By the end of the week, the bridge will reach the other shore.

These four words will follow you all through the new book. Each one is about what can happen to a country, and to the people in it, during a war. Read the sentence, take the word apart, then make your guess before you flip the card. Guessing first is how a word starts to belong to you.

Some words stand in for people: she, they, him, them. They don’t all do the same job. Some do the action, some receive it, and a couple can do both. Sort them by the job they’re doing, then name the groups yourself. Names you give stick better than names you’re given.

Long words from history often hide two vowels working together to make one sound. The trick is that the same pair doesn’t always sound the same. Say each word out loud, slowly, and listen for what the pair is really saying before you sort it. Your ear knows more than you think.

Here is one plain sentence about the end of the war. Your job is to say it three different ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. Writers have practiced this way for hundreds of years. Each new way shows you something the first sentence left out.

This quarter we watch for courage, and here is the first thing to know about it. Courage isn’t the same as not being scared. It’s being scared and doing the right thing anyway. Even reading about a hard time in history takes a little of that. If today’s facts feel heavy, that’s all right. Stay with them. That’s the first small brave thing.

The passage is short, and it covers six long years. Watch for two things: the countries that were taken over, one after another, and the countries that joined together to stop it. When you reach the pause questions, stop and think about a child your age living in one of those places.

Now it’s your turn to write. The questions ask you to go back to the passage, so keep it open beside you. Use the passage’s own facts, the dates and the names, to show how you know. Then you’ll finish with a short piece of your own writing.

These three questions build on each other. The first asks when and who. The second asks what was happening. The third asks who stood against it. Put them together, and you have the whole shape of the war in a few sentences. That shape is what you’ll carry into the novel.

Your writing project this quarter is an opinion essay, and it starts with one simple skill. A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks, and someone else could disagree. Today you’ll practice telling them apart, using things from your own life. Soon you’ll use the same skill on the new book.
Translate. To carry meaning across languages.
Protect. To cover in front; to shield.
